note: Week 9 lessons: the capstone: two case studies and your story. Each lesson has a level (basics, intermediate or advanced) so the climb is visible.

lessons.title: Polish case study 1: story, outcome, honest labels
lessons.inOneSentence: You will turn case study 1 from a draft into a finished piece: a sharp story, clear visuals, the feedback you received, and an honest outcome.
lessons.youCanNow: Revise the access-policy case study's story and outcome, labelling what was self-initiated, simulated or tested.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Hiring managers skim. A polished case study shows senior judgement through what you leave out as much as what you include. This is the piece that will start most of your interview conversations.
keyIdeas: Apply the feedback from Week 7 first; note what you changed and why.
Cut to the story: problem, insight, key decisions, result. Move process details to the end or remove them.
Make the first screen count: a title that states the problem, one strong image, and a one-paragraph summary.
Show impact even without launch: what the tests showed, the metric you would track, and what you would do next.
Add the senior layer: the trade-offs you made, how you would work with engineering and product, and how the design would scale to 5,000 devices.
Label it as a self-initiated concept and say who you researched and tested with.

words.meaning: The story structure that connects problem, decisions and result.
Easy to understand by skimming headings, images and captions.
How a design holds up with many more users, rules or devices.

steps.text: Read how hiring managers look at UX portfolios.
Apply the practitioner feedback and list what you changed.
Rewrite the opening and cut the draft by about a third.
Finish the visuals: one hero image, key screens with captions, one diagram.
Add a trade-offs and scale section, and a clear self-initiated label.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not add new features to the design now. Polish the story.
checkYourself: What is the one-sentence summary of case study 1?
Which trade-off shows your senior judgement best?
lookFor: A good summary names the user, the problem and the result, for example: “I designed a policy editor that shows admins who will gain or lose access before they save, and in testing both admins trusted the preview enough to save.”
A good answer names a real trade-off from your work and the evidence behind the choice, such as plain-language previews versus showing the full rule.

lessons.title: Polish case study 2: story, outcome, honest labels
lessons.inOneSentence: You will finish case study 2 to the same standard, making the technical subject easy to follow for any reader.
lessons.youCanNow: Revise the network-policy case study's story and outcome with accurate, honestly labelled claims.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Your second case study proves range: a different user (the platform engineer), a deeper technical domain and a rollout problem. Together the two pieces tell hiring managers you can work across identity and network security.
keyIdeas: Apply the Week 8 feedback and record the changes.
Explain Kubernetes network policy in one picture and one paragraph, for readers who do not know it.
Highlight what is unique: staged enforcement and trust in recommendations.
Show collaboration: what you learned from engineers and how it changed the design.
End with outcome and next steps: metrics, open questions and what you would test next.
Check consistency between the two case studies: structure, labels, image style.

words.meaning: Showing you can solve different kinds of problems.
Using the same structure and style across pieces so readers can compare.

steps.text: Apply the practitioner feedback and list what you changed.
Rewrite the opening and cut the draft by about a third.
Finish the visuals: hero image, key screens with captions, the network policy picture.
Check both case studies side by side for consistency.
Ask one person to read both openings and tell you what each is about.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not explain every Kubernetes term. Explain only what the reader needs to follow the story.
checkYourself: Can a non-technical reader understand the problem in case study 2 from its opening?
What does case study 2 show that case study 1 does not?
lookFor: A good answer is tested: someone outside the field read the opening and could explain the problem back in their own words.
For example: designing for a highly technical user, working with traffic data and recommendations, and designing a safe staged rollout in Kubernetes.

lessons.title: Portfolio page, LinkedIn and resume for identity and security roles
lessons.inOneSentence: You will present yourself as a product designer for identity and network security: portfolio home page, LinkedIn and resume, all telling the same story.
lessons.youCanNow: Write a portfolio page, LinkedIn summary and resume section positioned for identity/security product-design roles.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Recruiters and hiring managers at companies like Tailscale and Tigera search for specific signals: security domain knowledge, technical users, complex systems. Your materials should show these at a glance, backed by your two case studies.
keyIdeas: Your positioning sentence: who you design for and what you solve, for example “Product designer for identity and network security: I make access and infrastructure tools clear and safe.”
Portfolio home: the positioning sentence, the two case studies first, then other work.
LinkedIn: headline with your positioning, an About section with your story into the domain, and featured links to both case studies.
Resume: lead with relevant outcomes; add the domain skills you can now honestly claim (zero trust, SSO and SCIM, Kubernetes network policy, security UX).
Use real job posts: mirror their language where it is true for you.
Be honest about what you learned in this course and what you did in past roles. Specific and true beats impressive and vague.

words.meaning: A short statement of who you help and how.
The line under your name on LinkedIn.
LinkedIn’s section for highlighting links such as case studies.

steps.text: Re-read the portfolio guidance on how hiring managers scan.
Re-read two job posts and highlight the words that describe you truthfully.
Write and test your positioning sentence with one person.
Update your portfolio home page with both case studies first.
Update LinkedIn: headline, About and featured case studies.
Update your resume with domain skills and outcomes.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not rewrite your whole career history. Focus on the top third of each page.
checkYourself: Which three domain skills can you now honestly claim?
lookFor: A good sentence names who you design for and the value, in plain words, and matches the roles you want.
For example: zero-trust access policies, SSO and SCIM setup flows, Kubernetes network policy and security UX patterns, each backed by an exercise or case study.

lessons.title: Interview practice: a live design exercise and a retrospective
lessons.inOneSentence: You will practise the interviews you will face: presenting a case study, a live design exercise in this domain, and a retrospective on the 60 days.
lessons.youCanNow: Explain a security architecture in plain language, identify a risk in a live design exercise, and defend a design trade-off under questioning.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Senior interviews test how you think out loud, handle technical questions and take feedback. Practising with domain-specific prompts turns what you learned into confident answers.
keyIdeas: Case study presentation: 15 minutes, problem first, then key decisions and trade-offs, then results. Leave time for questions.
Live exercise prompts to practise: “Design how an admin finds out why an employee cannot reach a server” or “Design how an engineer rolls out a network policy safely”.
In live exercises, ask clarifying questions first (who, what scale, what constraints), then think aloud, sketch, and name trade-offs.
Expect domain questions: explain zero trust, SSO versus SCIM, default deny, or how an agent should be authorised. Your glossary is your study guide.
Retrospective: what you can do now that you could not on Day 1, what is still weak, and your next 30 days.

words.meaning: A live or take-home design problem used in interviews.
A question that narrows the problem before you start.
A look back at what went well, what did not, and what to change.

steps.text: Read about giving and receiving design critique.
Present one case study out loud in 15 minutes, recorded or to a friend, and note where you hesitated.
Do one live design exercise from the prompts above in 40 minutes, thinking aloud.
Answer five domain questions from your glossary out loud without notes.
Write your retrospective and your plan for the next 30 days.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not memorise scripts. Practise the structure, so you can adapt to any question.
checkYourself: What do you ask first in a live design exercise?
What can you do now that you could not do on Day 1?
lookFor: Clarifying questions: who the user is, what they are trying to do, at what scale, under which constraints and how success is measured. Then state your assumptions.
A good answer is specific, for example explaining zero trust and network policy in plain words, designing for admins and engineers, and presenting two case studies with evidence.
